title: Incisional hernia mesh selection
fairness: Report scope: the 11 new/revised executable drafts, each containing one decision node. Judgments use only each after Presentation, Exhibit, Task and Options; none has a separate Current update. Review-only key markers, explanations and author self-checks are not learner evidence. The four frozen prior PASS items are excluded. The 17 parked topics and one owner-held topic are noted but not graded; the disposition records are not additional executable questions. No network or fresh source verification was performed. Difficulty is a qualitative PGY-2/3 prediction. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval; all new versions remain needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version sign-off.

Node node.n4.ventral-controlled-enterotomy-mesh-material.v2: interpret the controlled bowel event together with the reconstructed pocket's relationship to bowel, then select an implant material. Mistaking this for direct visceral contact or treating any enterotomy as a reason to prefer biologic material produces distinct consequential errors. Moderate difficulty is credible.

Macroporous monofilament polypropylene is the defensible best of the offered materials for this expressly selected single-stage, closable, extraperitoneal reconstruction. The previously missing plane and closure information is now present. This judgment does not endorse single-stage repair for every enterotomy or claim that ePTFE is preferred in a contaminated intraperitoneal counterfactual.

No decisive nonmedical cue identified: the three options name concrete materials at comparable specificity, without a uniquely elaborate key, component convergence, diagnosis disclosure or a teaching sentence naming the polymer. The pocket description is necessary anatomical evidence.

Phase genuinely fits: source control and posterior-layer reconstruction have occurred, while the implant has not been selected. The current operative findings constrain the choice now. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the visible fields.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit selected-repair scope, primary-closure feasibility and separation of the prosthesis from bowel.
Keep the conclusion limited to this material comparison; do not extrapolate it into a universal timing or contamination rule. Obtain clinical sign-off on this exact version.

title: Unexpected upper-arm mass

cues.why: Minor favorable qualifier: only the key calls its biopsy planned. It makes that option sound more deliberate, but does not independently settle whether tissue should be obtained from the existing exposure now. This is not a decisive blind shortcut.

fairness: Node node.n4.unexpected-deep-mass-during-lipoma-excision.v2: reconcile the superficial ultrasound focus with the separate muscle-associated deep lump, then decide whether the unexpected lesion should be sampled or removed through the current exposure before local characterization. The incisional-biopsy alternative is a credible temptation because the wound is already open; the task now tests immediate tissue handling as well as investigation sequencing.

Closing without cutting the lesion, followed by regional MRI and a planned core biopsy, is the defensible best offered plan. The superficial fatty-appearing focus does not characterize the deeper operative target. A deep firm lesion is not itself proof of malignancy, and this review makes no such diagnostic claim.

Unlike the prior version, the three choices actually differ in what happens to the lesion during this operation. The later MRI does not have to occur intraoperatively for the decision to fit the phase: closing, incisional sampling and marginal excision are competing immediate actions.

Options have comparable scope and length, and the task is neutral. No diagnosis label or unique imaging-location match supplies the key. The ultrasound mismatch is useful evidence, although the unexpected deep anatomy would itself warrant reassessment even if the ultrasound row were removed.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This selected uncharacterized-lesion scenario does not establish that incisional biopsy is universally inappropriate; its suitability depends on prior characterization and biopsy planning absent here.
suggestions: Preserve the immediate close-versus-sample-versus-excise comparison and the separate superficial and deep targets.

Avoid adding praise-like planning qualifiers to only one option. Keep biopsy-route and specialist-planning details in appropriate feedback or clinically necessary shared context, without implying every incisional biopsy is an error.

title: Recurrent ulcer bleeding

cues.phrase: The previous clip arms have caught thin superficial edges that are separating from the base.
cues.why: A nonmedical reader can use failed-tool repetition to discount another through-the-scope clip. However, this does not distinguish deeper endoscopic capture from arterial embolization; the observation is necessary failure-mechanism evidence, not a sufficient answer shortcut.

fairness: Node node.n4.ulcer-recurrent-bleeding-after-clips.v2: infer inadequate superficial purchase rather than simply an untreated second vessel, then decide whether the accessible focal target supports a different capture strategy before ending endoscopic treatment. Repeating the prior tool and escalating immediately are recognizable competing errors.

A cap-mounted clip is the defensible best of the three offered strategies for this stabilized patient with recurrent focal bleeding and a stable frontal view. The view and tissue-response observations support considering additional endoscopic treatment, but do not guarantee successful capture or hemostasis.

The prior device-specific permission sentence has been replaced by observations. The options are concrete and similarly scoped; the task no longer grammatically excludes embolization. No convergence, diagnosis-label giveaway or uniquely qualified key is apparent.

Phase genuinely fits: the bleeding point and prior clip behavior are being observed during repeat endoscopy. The embolization choice explicitly ends this attempt, so it is a current escalation decision rather than a claim that embolization occurs through the endoscope.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Exact device suitability remains a clinician judgment; the item does not establish that another conventional clip could never work or that embolization is never appropriate.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between superficial clip purchase and the current focal access rather than reducing the item to recurrent bleeding followed by a device name.
Keep escalation phrased as the decision to end the current attempt. Do not convert the tissue observations into an assurance that the lesion can be drawn into the keyed device.

title: Pedunculated polyp resection

cues.phrase: Hot-snare transection followed by rescue clipping
cues.why: The word rescue frames this as reacting to a complication, whereas the key presents an orderly preventive sequence. It is a weak preventive-versus-reactive heuristic, not a complete nonmedical proof; the actual bleeding-risk comparison still requires clinical knowledge.

cues.phrase: Surface vessels run up the stalk into the head
cues.why: This explicitly spotlights the structure addressed by pre-transection ligation. It is an anatomical observation rather than a false teaching claim, but adds a preventive-hemostasis hint without a separate competing inference.

fairness: Node node.n4.pedunculated-polyp-head-versus-stalk.v2: the broad stalk makes preventive hemostasis before hot-snare transection the plausible best offered sequence. The head and stalk are already explicitly identified and measured; there is no unresolved morphology interpretation.

For PGY-2/3 residents this principally applies one pedunculated-polyp prophylaxis rule. Distinguishing head size from stalk width is useful, but recognition of the supplied stalk measurement followed by its familiar procedural sequence does not establish two consequential reasoning steps. The cold-snare alternative is not a close competitor for the described broad-stalked lesion.

The three options have similar length and concrete actions; no component convergence or uniquely elaborate key is evident. Antithrombotic negatives remove an additional explanation for bleeding risk rather than create a second decision.

Phase genuinely fits: the lesion is still attached during colonoscopy and the selected sequence changes what is done before transection. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified and no new numerical threshold asserted. Exact loop suitability cannot be fully assessed from width alone; this is a technical-feasibility uncertainty for clinician review, not proof that the key is wrong.
suggestions: Either seek explicit acceptance as a basic prophylaxis-rule item or redesign around a verified technical finding that changes which of several credible current resection/hemostasis plans is appropriate.

For a harder revision, make the consequential choice depend on actual attachment geometry or a treatment constraint and supply the observations needed to judge it. Do not manufacture a stalk-length cutoff or device rule.

Describe the competing post-transection hemostasis plan neutrally, including its contingency if intended, instead of relying on rescue as a negative qualifier. Reassess distractor plausibility after the clinical objective is fixed.

title: Biopsy after food-bolus extraction

cues.why: The task requests action before completing the current examination, which grammatically disadvantages the option Esophageal biopsies after proton-pump inhibitor treatment. This narrows the set without interpreting the esophageal findings.

cues.phrase: the mucosa there has not been contacted by the extraction device
cues.why: Together with the explicitly abraded extraction patch, this supplies the clean-versus-traumatized sampling contrast in near-rationale form. Once the delayed option is excluded, the key's away from the extraction patch phrasing closely follows that contrast.

fairness: Node node.n4.post-impaction-biopsy-site-versus-trauma.v2: multilevel samples away from the extraction injury are the defensible best offered plan for the recurrent dysphagia and distributed findings. Sampling the traumatized patch is not equivalent to obtaining representative samples for the suspected underlying process.

All options now concern the esophagus, repairing the old organ-location giveaway. However, the lead-in excludes the timing competitor and leaves a readily apparent injured-versus-uninjured sampling comparison. For PGY-2/3 residents the visible sequence does not require two consequential inferences.

Removing the detailed grooves/ridges description would still leave recurrent food impaction and a traumatic extraction site favoring the same plan among these choices. The added findings strengthen suspicion but do not create the proposed harder sampling decision.

Phase genuinely fits: extraction is complete, the examination is ongoing and biopsy timing/site remain actionable. Deferring biopsies can also be a decision made now, but the task must allow that alternative neutrally rather than disqualify it grammatically.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. No biopsy-count requirement or medication washout interval is inferred. The review does not claim that every extraction site is unsafe to sample; the concern here is representativeness for this diagnostic question.
suggestions: Use a neutral task such as choosing the diagnostic sampling plan after bolus removal, allowing both current and deferred plans to answer it.

Retain the real injury and distributed mucosal observations, but compare credible sampling/timing errors whose ranking requires interpreting the findings, rather than announcing that the alternative territory was untouched.

If the repaired item remains routine representative-biopsy selection, seek explicit basic-item acceptance. Do not obscure the extraction injury or invent biopsy numbers, treatment intervals or contraindications to manufacture difficulty.

title: Bilateral testis position
fairness: Node node.n4.bilateral-testis-maintenance-versus-ascent.v2: the left testis can remain dependently without tension, while the right cannot remain scrotal on repeated relaxed examination. Left surveillance and right operative planning are the defensible best offered combination. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The four-option matrix is genuinely balanced: each side/action component occurs equally often. There is no majority-component convergence, uniquely qualified answer or diagnosis label. The mirrored wrong-side option is mainly an attention error, but its presence does not make the matrix unfair.

The limitation is cognitive depth. These are two parallel, classic examination-to-management associations, not two consequential steps within a residual decision. A resident can independently assign each side its familiar action and combine them. The earlier bilateral scrotal documentation changes the historical classification but not the offered management choice given the current examinations.

Clinic phase, repeated examination and caregiver context fit. Essential position, tension and release behavior are present; removing them would damage fairness. No exact surveillance interval or acquired-ascent treatment deadline is supplied or inferred.
suggestions: Preserve the balanced matrix and the raw examination findings. Do not synonym-swap or pad the options to hide their deliberate symmetry.

Either accept this explicitly as basic side-specific examination-to-management practice or use a verified longitudinal/examination discrepancy that changes a remaining decision rather than merely adding a second side.
A harder revision should make the new evidence necessary to rank credible current plans; repeating the same positional rule twice is not sufficient.

title: Cholecystectomy dissection before division

cues.phrase: The inferior gallbladder surface remains apposed to the liver.
cues.why: This names the unfinished attachment corresponding directly to Separate the lower gallbladder to expose its cystic plate. A reader can match an unseparated surface to separation without resolving much of the operative anatomy.

cues.phrase: not the gallbladder’s attachment surface behind them
cues.why: This is an explicit missing-view statement that points toward the only option exposing that surface. It is necessary safety information, but the present option set turns the omission into the answer.

fairness: Node node.n4.two-tubes-versus-liver-bed-separation.v1: further lower-gallbladder separation to expose the cystic plate is the defensible best offered step before division. Seeing two tubes is not equivalent to having established all necessary anatomical relationships. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The item chiefly recognizes an explicitly missing component of the safety view and supplies that component. The tube count is a familiar competing shortcut, while tracing to the common bile duct is a weak alternative for residents who know the intended safety method. This is easy safety/checklist application rather than two consequential steps.

The traction row is useful operative information but does not rescue the option set: deleting it still leaves one constructive completion step, premature division and unnecessary duct tracing. It does not force a choice between two credible ways to proceed when the attachment cannot be separated safely.

Phase genuinely fits: no structure has been divided, and the observations concern the current dissection. The key should be understood as careful further dissection and reassessment, not permission to persist through an unsafe plane.
suggestions: Retain the information showing why division is not justified; do not hide a missing safety view to make the question harder.
Seek explicit acceptance as a basic operative-safety item, or compare verified same-phase options whose ranking actually depends on the observed dissection response and remaining anatomy.

If anatomy interpretation is the objective, a reviewed original operative schematic could carry the spatial evidence more naturally than an explicit missing-component sentence. An image alone will not repair weak distractors.

title: Incomplete intraoperative cholangiogram

cues.phrase: the corresponding branching pattern on the other side is outside the opacified field
cues.why: This makes incomplete coverage conspicuous and favors obtaining better imaging. It is necessary study-adequacy evidence rather than an instruction to de-air. Deciding why free duodenal flow is insufficient still requires clinical interpretation; this is not a decisive nonmedical shortcut.

fairness: Node node.n4.cholangiogram-lucencies-and-proximal-coverage.v1: interpret the moving/deforming lucencies as insufficient proof of stones and the unilateral proximal filling as insufficient anatomical coverage, then choose to improve the on-table study before exploration or completion. Treating apparent filling defects and treating distal flow as proof of adequacy are credible competing errors.

De-airing and repeating ductal imaging is the defensible best next plan among those offered. The observations do not prove that every lucency is air, that no stone exists, or that the cannulated structure has been correctly identified. Repetition must resolve the proximal anatomy as well as reassess the defects.

There is no air label or named keyed maneuver in the exhibit, and all choices answer the current operative-plan task. No unique length, favorable qualification or component-convergence cue is apparent.

The two exhibit features are not both indispensable: incomplete proximal coverage alone can justify further imaging. Thus this PASS supports interpretation of study adequacy followed by a consequential operative decision, not a claim that two independent diagnoses must be solved or that bubble recognition is separately assessed.

Phase genuinely fits: the duct is cannulated, the current acquisition is unresolved and further on-table imaging can change whether to proceed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The exact repeat-acquisition technique remains a clinician matter; this report invents no injection or flushing protocol.
suggestions: Preserve the requirement to resolve proximal anatomy; do not reduce the key to clearing bubbles and then accepting duodenal flow as sufficient.
A reviewed original sequential cholangiogram schematic would better test image interpretation, but must preserve essential accessible observations without labelling air bubbles or duct identity.
Keep the objective described as study interpretation and the next operative action, without overstating the independent contribution of each row.

title: Recurrent groin repair after anterior exposure

cues.why: This is the only laparoscopic and only non-anterior-labelled option. Both alternatives begin Open anterior. That repeated shared category makes the key the conspicuous outlier before the mesh/cord relationships are interpreted; it is a heuristic rather than proof.

cues.phrase: Dense scar joins the mesh edge to the cord.
cues.why: The explicit scar hazard favors the sole different-approach option. This is clinically relevant evidence, but two anterior competitors make avoidance of the described scar too easy to infer without locating the prior mesh plane.

fairness: Node node.n4.recurrent-groin-mesh-compartment.v1: the potential substantive chain is to infer a prior anterior repair from the mesh, floor and cord relationships, then choose a posterior repair rather than repeat work in that scarred compartment. That can be moderately difficult; the category structure currently weakens the assessment.

TAPP is the plausible best offered definitive repair for recurrence after the described anterior repair. The visible evidence does not make anterior Lichtenstein and Shouldice equally attractive alternatives. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted about the general posterior-after-anterior principle.

Phase is only partially established. The exposure and scar are real current operative observations, and a change of approach could genuinely be decided now. However, nothing says the previous repair plane was unknown or different from expected, or explains why an anterior incision was begun before this choice. The discriminating principle could have selected the approach preoperatively; calling the findings Current exposure does not establish a newly arising decision.

Switching from the already opened anterior operation to TAPP also depends on the actual operative setting. Its feasibility is not established by the visible fields. This is an unresolved same-operation ranking/context concern, not a claim that conversion is impossible or that a blanket capability permission sentence should be added.
Do not assume that more detailed anterior scar prose creates a new two-step intraoperative decision. The item needs a reason the new observation changes a previously reasonable plan.
suggestions: Move this to preoperative recurrent-repair planning, or establish a genuine unexpected operative finding that changes the current approach and the specific context needed to make that change feasible.
Compare credible same-stage plans at balanced specificity; avoid using two near-equivalent anterior-category errors merely to leave a single conspicuous posterior option.

If retained intraoperatively, make the immediate handling of the existing exposure and the subsequent repair path clear enough to rank the options. Obtain clinician review of that exact conversion scenario.

title: Lumpectomy target remaining in breast

cues.phrase: The top-hat marker and calcification cluster remain together immediately medial to the excision cavity.
cues.why: This explicitly locates the unremoved intended target outside the specimen. Targeted re-excision follows by ordinary goal matching; neither repeating pictures of the removed specimen nor closing addresses that plainly stated remaining target.

cues.phrase: Complete closure and await permanent histologic margins
cues.why: After the exhibit explicitly says the target remains in the breast, this option advertises stopping before accomplishing the named operation. It is a weak competitor rather than a close margin-management error.

fairness: Node node.n4.lumpectomy-marker-identity-and-target.v1: targeted further excision with specimen radiography is the defensible best offered current plan. Repeating views of the first specimen does not retrieve a target independently localized in the breast. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The current localization row resolves the proposed marker-identity puzzle before the choice. Removing the benign coil history and most of the specimen-marker comparison still leaves the target explicitly in the breast and the same answer. Matching two marker shapes therefore is not a consequential first step for this version.

The options are concrete and reasonably parallel, but the reassuring-marker error has already been defeated by an explicit target-location result. This is easy target-retrieval recognition, not a moderate two-step specimen interpretation problem.

Phase genuinely fits: the first specimen has been removed and the wound is not yet closed. The key concerns retrieval of the intended radiographic target, not a microscopic margin threshold. No inference about final margin adequacy or mandatory mastectomy is justified.
suggestions: Either accept this as basic target-retrieval safety practice or redesign the localization/specimen evidence so reconciling it is necessary to choose between credible further imaging and targeted operative work.
Do not simply delete the current localization result while retaining an unsupported targeted-excision key. Supply the actual observations that resolve the remaining uncertainty fairly.

A reviewed original marker/specimen map can test the spatial relationship without an answer-like location summary. Ensure the exhibit changes the decision and does not merely decorate the same obvious choice.

title: Intermittent pediatric groin swelling

cues.phrase: The bulge returns into the abdomen with gentle pressure. The abdomen is soft, the groin is not tender, and he has continued eating and passing stool.
cues.why: The cluster of reassuring observations makes Arrange emergency groin exploration readily dismissible even without detailed pediatric surgical knowledge. These are necessary urgency findings to retain, but they leave a weak emergency competitor.

cues.phrase: bowel sounds are heard over the bulge today
cues.why: Alongside the loop-shaped moving structure, this strongly announces enteric rather than fluid-only contents. It is a raw clinical observation, not literally a diagnosis label, but substantially pre-resolves the hydrocele-versus-hernia distinction for a resident.

fairness: Node node.n4.intermittent-groin-contents-versus-fluid-scan.v1: planned inguinal herniotomy is the defensible best offered plan for the current reducible enteric groin findings without the described signs of an acute complication. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in that ranking.

The quiet fluid-only scan does not create a necessary second inference: deleting the entire previous-ultrasound sentence leaves the same straightforward diagnosis and disposition. The task remains familiar reducible-hernia recognition followed by routine elective-versus-emergency triage.

The options compare three plans, but continued hydrocele follow-up is contradicted by the current findings and emergency exploration is contradicted by reducibility and the reassuring course. Neither offers a close residual decision for a PGY-2/3 resident. twoStep is false under the owner's consequential-reasoning standard, despite the nominal diagnose-then-treat sequence.

The parent video describes an externally visible loop-shaped movement, not verified anatomical contents. It should not be treated as direct visualization of bowel through the skin. The current clinical examination already carries the decision, so this uncertain interpretation is unnecessary to defend the key; no confident claim of physical impossibility is made.

Clinic phase, named child and caregiver fit. No treatment deadline or age cutoff is inferred. The unspecified duration of a hypothetical hydrocele would also prevent this item from teaching a general observation policy for hydroceles at this age.
suggestions: Retain reducibility, tenderness and obstructive-symptom information. Seek explicit acceptance as basic recognition/triage, or develop a verified residual decision that these findings do not already settle.
Make any prior imaging discrepancy necessary to the revised choice; otherwise remove it rather than counting historical conflict as an additional reasoning step.

Describe a parent video as observable swelling behavior without claiming it establishes tissue identity. Use credible current plans rather than a fluid-only diagnosis and an unsupported emergency operation as the main distractors.
